codex.worst_flaw: The launch-blocking safety gap is that crews can earn rewards for skipped safety checks because the audit verifies timestamps and required entries without independently checking whether technicians performed the checks.

claude.worst_flaw: Crew-level 70% goals ignore baseline differences between crews and include outages and paper fallbacks in the denominator, so a crew with poor-signal routes can fail through no fault of its own. Audit and appeals also lack replayable event and policy versioning or independent shadow validation of the counting rule.

holistic.reason: Union co-design, paid setup, private feedback, randomized stagger, fixed end date and clear audit/pause rules make it approvable and trustworthy, but it is dense, relies on timestamp data integrity, and the meal reward is modest, so awareness is moderate and durability hinges on the app fixes sticking.

codex.worst_flaw: Launch should wait until safety audits cover paper and missing checks and independently verify credited checks, since reviewing records for credited visits alone can miss skipped checks and unreported hazards.

claude.worst_flaw: The crew-level 65% group reward hits zero-opportunity weeks, technicians with uneven or very small job volume, and excused absences without clear rules, and corrections have no replayable event history and no independent appeal beyond the coordinator.

holistic.reason: Union-aware, pilot-first, measurement-hardened design with a strong default-based persistence plan and sensible safeguards, but a 30-minute paid-time crew reward is modest for a jump from 35% to 65%, and the sampling and verification burden is optimistic at under an hour a week.

claude.worst_flaw: The 80% goal and the 75%/60% stop thresholds are not tied to a diagnosed baseline or to what is feasible, and the design never settles statistical power, how crews are randomised across shared routes or spillover between waves, or what a 10-check weekly sample can detect across 300 technicians.

codex.worst_flaw: The routine safety audit samples only credited jobs, so technicians starting work without a checklist can escape review unless an incident brings those jobs to light.

holistic.reason: Union-co-designed, workflow-first, safety-protective (holds earn credit, paper fallback, audits, pause rule) with a randomized staggered rollout and clear stop thresholds, though the 80% goal, record-timestamp reliability, and a modest 30-minute reward limit visibility and durable effect.

claude.worst_flaw: The team-level 80% metric has no per-reviewer opportunity normalisation or uneven load handling, and the learning design cannot isolate the reward's value over the queue fixes when there is a single shared queue. The design also gives no sample size or uncertainty plan.

codex.worst_flaw: If the team shares one review queue, the trial cannot distinguish the effect of the paid-hour reward from the effect of the workflow fixes and private feedback.

holistic.reason: Fixing the queue first, using a team-level reward and the quality check suit sceptical engineers, but the plan has many moving parts and a single paid hour is a weak hook, so awareness and lasting change hinge on the workflow fixes sticking.

codex.worst_flaw: The shared-queue pilot introduces the reward alongside workflow changes without a feedback-only comparison, so any improvement cannot establish whether the reward adds value.

claude.worst_flaw: The eight-working-hour clock and 85% shared target are not justified against the baseline or reviewer capacity. The design does not account for uneven reviewer load, specialist-only PRs or time-zone spread, so the team could miss or game the target. Learning also rests on an optional staggered rollout that, with one queue, gives only a confounded before/after reading.

holistic.reason: It fixes the real bottleneck first, uses a sceptic-friendly shared reward with private individual data and no leaderboard, and has a clear exit rule; but the eight-hour credit rule, sampling overhead and the modest lunch reward make it somewhat complex and low-salience.

claude.worst_flaw: The two-group randomized stagger is too small to support causal inference: it has no plan for uncertainty or a minimum detectable effect, no cost or harm thresholds for the decision, and no cleanly isolated comparison of the reward against plain queue fixes.

codex.worst_flaw: The two-group pilot gives the reward only two weeks of comparison against plain feedback and sets no minimum PR volume, case-mix adjustment, or decision rule for judging its added value.

holistic.reason: Fixes the queue and routing first, uses a modest team reward with private feedback and anti-gaming checks, and ends with a clear stagger and follow-up test, but the counting rules and weekly sampling add overhead and the rewards are low-salience for sceptical engineers.

codex.worst_flaw: The design is not launchable as specified because wards can meet both reward and retention targets by improving logging during observed audits while routine documentation remains unchanged.

claude.worst_flaw: The reward depends on a measure that observers must check by confirming entries with nurses during care, yet the design has no event log, replayable record, correction history or staffed appeal process. It also never defines what an excused miss is (for example a kiosk outage or an emergency) beyond the fallback, and it doesn't say how a ward recovers after it misses its two-audit window.

holistic.reason: Well-designed with strong safety guardrails, a verification step, and a staggered rollout, but the single team meal is a weak, delayed incentive, the audit-dependent measurement is heavy, and the workflow-fix and default-kiosk changes carry more of the lasting effect than the reward does.

codex.worst_flaw: A single audit of 15–20 completed actions can decide whether the workflow is kept or dropped, even when the result is driven by sampling variation or saves that observers could not verify.

claude.worst_flaw: The adoption measure asks nurses after care to say whether they saved each observed action, which is a small, self-reported sample that may not be independent, and the design never checks kiosk entries against audited opportunities or looks for inflated or fabricated logging.

holistic.reason: Well-designed with team-level rewards tied to existing audits, worker input, failure-case handling and a stopping rule, but the extra kiosk burden, small three-ward sample and a reward that ends may blunt motivation and durability.

claude.worst_flaw: The primary kiosk-use metric (shifts with at least one saved entry) can't tell real logging of hand-hygiene moments from token entries, so it doesn't measure the behaviour the hospital wants, and nothing reconciles it with the opportunity-based audit data.

codex.worst_flaw: The launch decision gives a shift full credit for one saved entry, so the pilot cannot establish whether nurses reliably log eligible hand-hygiene moments.

holistic.reason: Rewarding a team-level workflow fix rather than logging volume is safe and sensibly paired with audit checks and a clear keep/retire rule, but it is complex and hard to explain, and a shared team meal is a weak pull that most nurses may not notice, though fixing the kiosk friction could help the habit last.

codex.worst_flaw: The same 40% reward threshold applies to every team even though some teams may resolve more tickets with no safe or useful article, making the reward depend on case mix and creating pressure to attach unsuitable articles.

claude.worst_flaw: The design says every resolved ticket should get an article but sets a 40% team target and counts every resolved ticket in the denominator, including tickets where no useful article exists. It never handles case mix or leave, and its randomised comparison uses only a few intact teams over two weeks with no plan for uncertainty or spillover, so the measured effect would not be reliable.

holistic.reason: Fixes workflow friction first, rewards useful rather than any attachments, keeps CSAT intact, and has quality audits, a staggered-start comparison and a clear keep/revise/drop rule, but the lunch reward is modest and the counting rules are complex enough to feel bureaucratic.

codex.worst_flaw: The 9-of-10 audit can pass even when it finds a customer-information leak, with no specified containment or payout pause for that breach.

claude.worst_flaw: The keep, adjust or drop decision uses the change from the team's own baseline, not the difference from the comparison group. With only about 60 agents in a few intact teams, the two-week staggered comparison cannot separate the effect of the voucher from the effect of the workflow fixes or from a general trend.

holistic.reason: Well-designed with friction removal first, quality sampling, staggered rollout and clear decision rules, but a modest shared team voucher is a weak motivator, the two-week discovery delay and heavy measurement overhead add risk, and lasting change depends mainly on the workflow defaults rather than the reward.

codex.worst_flaw: The reward threshold includes tickets where an article would be inappropriate, making meal eligibility depend partly on case mix and creating pressure to attach unsuitable links.

claude.worst_flaw: The design never says how absences, leave or outages are treated in the four-week per-agent goal, and it never addresses small books, case mix or uneven volume across teams for the 35% team milestone. A team or agent with unusual ticket mix or time off can miss the goal unfairly, and nothing stops the team-level pressure from pushing marginal links.

holistic.reason: Well-designed with barrier removal, quality sampling, a staggered comparison and pre-checked measurement, but it is complex to run for a 60-person team, offers only a modest team-meal reward with a thin individual incentive, and the durability rests mainly on the workflow fixes sticking after prizes end.
